svg.aria-label: Image processing pipeline: an input photograph is converted to grayscale, resized to 128 by 128, tiled into 256 non-overlapping 8 by 8 patches, each patch flattened and L2-normalised into a 64-amplitude state, and all 32,640 admissible patch pairs formed with their displacement.

g.text: Figure 2 — Image Processing: photograph to quantum states
every operation performed on pixels before anything quantum happens
ψ₀ , ψ₁ ∈ ℝ⁶⁴ (two normalised patch vectors) + Δ = (dy, dx) / 128 (their displacement) — repeated for all 32,640 pairs
No descriptor is computed. No DCT, no histogram, no keypoints, no edges. The circuit receives raw normalised pixels and nothing else,
which is what makes the model “pure”: no classical algorithm has decided in advance which parts of the patch matter.
Why the pair count dominates everything
N patches produce N(N−1)/2 pairs, and each pair costs one circuit evaluation (32 ms). 256 patches → 32,640 pairs → ≈ 17 min per image.
Halving the patch size quadruples N and multiplies the pair count by ≈16 — so working resolution, not gate count, sets the runtime.
Stride is set EQUAL to patch size so the tiles cover the image completely.
With a larger stride the tiles leave gaps: at 256 px with stride 32, only 3 of 64 patches fell inside a 2%-area forged region,
and a forged image and its authentic original produced byte-identical output because the forgery was never sampled.
